title: DNA, RNA, protein synthesis and mutation
blurb: Describe DNA and RNA, apply base pairing, follow replication, transcription and translation codon by codon, and classify mutations by their effect.
question: In sickle cell anemia, a single base change in the hemoglobin gene swaps one amino acid for another. How does a DNA sequence become a protein, where does each step happen, and why does one changed base change the protein while some other base changes do not?

teach.body: Formal definition: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double helix of two antiparallel strands built from nucleotides (phosphate + deoxyribose + nitrogenous base); it stores genetic information. Watson and Crick described it in 1953, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data. In eukaryotes it wraps around histone proteins to form chromatin and chromosomes. A gene is a DNA segment that codes for a protein. Plain English: DNA is a twisted ladder; the sides are sugar and phosphate, and each rung is a pair of bases whose order spells out the instructions.

rows.label: Location
values: Made in nucleus; works in cytoplasm too

teach.caption: Backbone: covalent (phosphodiester) bonds. Rungs: hydrogen bonds between paired bases.

teach.body: A pairs with T (2 hydrogen bonds) and G pairs with C (3 hydrogen bonds); in RNA, U replaces T and pairs with A. A purine (A, G: double ring) always pairs with a pyrimidine (C, T, U: single ring). So in double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C. Worked example: if A = 30%, then T = 30%, leaving 40% for G and C together, so G = 20% and C = 20%.

steps.label: Helicase
steps.sub: Unzips the helix: breaks base-pair H-bonds

steps.label: Ligase
steps.sub: Joins fragments on the lagging strand

steps.label: Two helices
steps.sub: Each = one old strand + one new strand

teach.caption: Replication is semiconservative: each new DNA molecule keeps one original strand.

teach.h: Central dogma: DNA to RNA to protein

steps.label: Transcription
steps.sub: Nucleus: RNA polymerase copies a gene into mRNA

steps.label: mRNA exits
steps.sub: Through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm

steps.label: Translation
steps.sub: Ribosome reads codons; tRNA brings amino acids

steps.label: Protein
steps.sub: Peptide bonds link the amino acids

teach.caption: Replication and transcription happen in the nucleus; translation happens on ribosomes, free in the cytoplasm or on the rough ER.

head: RNA
Full name
Job
rows: Carries the code as codons to the ribosome
Brings a specific amino acid; has the anticodon
Structural and catalytic part of ribosomes

teach.body: mRNA is read three bases at a time; each triplet is a codon. There are 64 codons: 61 code for the 20 amino acids and 3 are stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA). AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine. The code is redundant (most amino acids have several codons), unambiguous (each codon has one meaning) and nearly universal. Worked chain: DNA template TAC is transcribed to mRNA AUG, which pairs with the tRNA anticodon UAC, which carries methionine.

head: Mutation
What changes
Effect on protein
rows: One base; creates a stop codon
Insertion or deletion, not a multiple of 3
teach.caption: Causes: copying errors and mutagens (UV light, X-rays, some chemicals). Germ-line mutations can be inherited; somatic mutations are not passed on.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Priya traces sickle cell
teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, follows the hemoglobin gene. In the nucleus, RNA polymerase transcribes the gene into mRNA, introns are removed, and the mRNA moves to ribosomes in the cytoplasm. There each codon pairs with a tRNA anticodon, and peptide bonds join the amino acids. In sickle cell anemia one base is substituted, so one codon now codes for valine instead of glutamic acid: a missense mutation. Had the new codon still coded for glutamic acid, the mutation would have been silent.

teach.text: Exam traps: RNA has URACIL, DNA has THYMINE; pairs are A-T and G-C; if A = 30%, G is 20%, not 30%; transcription is in the NUCLEUS, translation at RIBOSOMES; mRNA carries CODONS, tRNA the ANTIcodon; AUG STARTS translation; introns are REMOVED, exons kept; not every mutation changes the protein; deleting THREE bases removes one amino acid without a frameshift.

items: DNA: double helix, antiparallel, deoxyribose, A-T and G-C; RNA: single strand, ribose, uracil.
Replication is semiconservative: helicase unzips, DNA polymerase builds, ligase joins.
Transcription (nucleus, RNA polymerase) makes mRNA; introns removed before export.
Translation (ribosome): codons of 3 bases; tRNA anticodons; AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop.
64 codons, 20 amino acids: the code is redundant, unambiguous, nearly universal.
Mutations: silent, missense, nonsense, frameshift (indels not in multiples of 3), chromosomal.

summary: You can now describe DNA and RNA, apply the base-pairing rules and Chargaff's percentages, and explain semiconservative replication. You can also follow a gene through transcription and translation codon by codon and classify a mutation as silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift by its effect on the protein.

A.q: Which enzyme builds mRNA from a DNA template during transcription?
A.why: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand and builds a complementary mRNA in the nucleus.

whyNot.0: DNA polymerase builds new DNA during replication, not RNA.
whyNot.2: Helicase unwinds DNA during replication; it does not build a strand.
whyNot.3: Ligase joins DNA fragments during replication.

A.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
A.why: A = T = 30%, so A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is split equally between G and C, so G = 20%.

whyNot.0: 30% is the thymine value (T = A); guanine matches cytosine, not adenine.
whyNot.1: 40% is G and C combined; guanine is half of that.
whyNot.3: 70% is everything except adenine, not the guanine share.

A.q: Which molecule carries an anticodon and delivers a specific amino acid to the ribosome?
A.why: tRNA has an anticodon that pairs with an mRNA codon, and it carries the matching amino acid.

whyNot.0: mRNA carries the codons that the anticodons pair with.
whyNot.1: rRNA forms the structure and catalytic core of the ribosome; it does not ferry amino acids.
whyNot.2: DNA polymerase is an enzyme that builds new DNA during replication.

B.q: What holds the two strands of a DNA double helix together?
options: Peptide bonds between the base pairs
Ionic bonds between the two sugars
B.why: Complementary bases on opposite strands are joined by hydrogen bonds (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C).

whyNot.1: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, not DNA bases.
whyNot.2: Covalent (phosphodiester) bonds hold each strand's backbone, not the pairs across the middle.
whyNot.3: The sugars are in the backbones on the outside and are not bonded across to each other.

B.q: A DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. Which mRNA sequence is transcribed from it?
B.why: Transcription pairs T with A, A with U, C with G and G with C: TAC becomes AUG and GGA becomes CCU.

whyNot.0: mRNA contains uracil, not thymine, so T cannot appear in it.
whyNot.1: This copies the template (with U for T) instead of pairing with it.
whyNot.2: The last base is wrong: the template's A pairs with U in mRNA, not with A.

B.q: During DNA replication, which enzyme unzips the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between bases?
B.why: Helicase unwinds the helix and separates the strands so each can serve as a template.

whyNot.1: DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides after the strands are separated.
whyNot.2: Ligase seals gaps between DNA fragments.
whyNot.3: RNA polymerase transcribes RNA; it is not the replication unzipper.

C.q: A mutation deletes one base near the start of a gene's coding region. Why is this usually more harmful than a single-base substitution?
options: It changes one amino acid in the chain.
It shifts the reading frame of later codons.
It stops the cell from replicating its DNA.
It turns the start codon into a stop codon.
C.why: Codons are read in threes. Deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is misread: a frameshift.

whyNot.0: Changing one amino acid describes a missense substitution, usually less harmful.
whyNot.2: A deletion in one gene does not stop the whole genome from replicating.
whyNot.3: A deletion near the start does not necessarily hit the start codon; the damage comes from the frameshift.

C.q: A double-stranded DNA segment contains 200 bases, 60 of which are cytosine. How many of its bases are adenine?
C.why: C = 60, so G = 60, giving 120. That leaves 200 - 120 = 80 for A + T, and A = T, so A = 40.

whyNot.0: 60 is the guanine count (G = C), not adenine.
whyNot.1: 70 comes from (200 - 60) / 2, which forgets that guanine also equals 60.
whyNot.3: 80 is adenine and thymine combined; adenine is half of that.

C.q: A substitution changes the mRNA codon GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What type of mutation is this?
C.why: Because the code is redundant, the new codon still codes for glycine: the protein is unchanged, a silent mutation.

whyNot.0: A missense mutation changes the amino acid; here it stays glycine.
whyNot.1: A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon; GGC codes for glycine.
whyNot.2: A frameshift needs an insertion or deletion; this is a one-base substitution.

reteach.title: The library's master cookbook
reteach.question: Imagine a library cookbook that can never leave the reading room. How does a kitchen still cook from it?

blocks.body: The master cookbook (DNA) stays in the reading room (nucleus). A librarian (RNA polymerase) photocopies one recipe (transcription) and trims the notes that are not steps (introns). The copy (mRNA) goes to the kitchen (ribosome), where the recipe is read in three-letter words (codons). Kitchen helpers (tRNA) each bring one ingredient (amino acid) matched to a word. A typo can change nothing (silent), swap one ingredient (missense), end the recipe early (nonsense) or scramble every word after it (frameshift).

blocks.text: The cookbook never goes to the kitchen: DNA stays in the nucleus, and only the mRNA copy travels to the ribosome.

explain.body: Each strand is a sugar-phosphate backbone with bases pointing inward. A pairs with T, G with C, and the strands run in opposite directions (antiparallel), so the partner strand is the complement read the other way.

test.q: One strand of DNA reads 5'-ATGCCA-3'. What is the complementary strand, written 3' to 5'?
test.why: A pairs with T and G with C, so ATGCCA pairs with TACGGT, running in the opposite direction.

whyNot.0: Uracil appears in RNA, not DNA.
whyNot.2: This pairs A with G and T with C, which is not how DNA bases pair.
whyNot.3: This is the original strand written backward, not its complement.

explain.body: In S phase, helicase unzips the DNA, DNA polymerase builds a complementary strand on each old strand and proofreads, and ligase joins fragments. Each daughter helix is half old, half new.

test.q: After one round of DNA replication, each new double helix contains:
options: One original and one new strand
test.why: Replication is semiconservative: each helix keeps one original strand and gains one new strand.

whyNot.0: Rejoined original strands would be conservative replication, which does not happen.
whyNot.1: Each helix keeps one parent strand as its template.
whyNot.3: Mixed pieces within each strand would be dispersive replication, which was ruled out.

explain.body: Transcription in the nucleus makes mRNA; introns are cut out. At the ribosome, each mRNA codon pairs with a tRNA anticodon carrying one amino acid. Start at AUG; stop at UAA, UAG or UGA.

test.q: An mRNA codon reads AUG. Which tRNA anticodon pairs with it?
test.why: The anticodon is complementary to the codon in RNA bases: A pairs with U and G with C, so AUG pairs with UAC.

whyNot.0: An anticodon is complementary to the codon, not identical to it.
whyNot.1: TAC is the DNA template sequence; tRNA uses uracil, not thymine.
whyNot.3: ATG is a DNA sequence; RNA contains no thymine.

explain.body: Substitutions can be silent (same amino acid), missense (one different amino acid) or nonsense (a premature stop). Insertions or deletions not in multiples of three cause frameshifts. Only germ-line mutations are inherited.

test.q: Which type of point mutation creates a premature stop codon?
test.why: A nonsense mutation turns an amino-acid codon into a stop codon, cutting the protein short.

whyNot.0: A missense mutation swaps in a different amino acid; the chain continues.
whyNot.2: A silent mutation keeps the same amino acid.
whyNot.3: An inversion is a chromosomal mutation that flips a whole segment, not a single-base change.
